transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Benchmark report launch - post-launch retro / metrics readout
Date: Mar 6, 2025 4:00 PM PT
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees:
- Ben Carter (Redwood, Growth / Campaign Owner)
- Camila Reyes (Redwood, Marketing Exec Sponsor)
- Talia Benson (Redwood, Program Mgmt)
- Tyler Benson (Redwood, Marketing Ops)
- Ethan Wallace (Redwood, Report author / narrative)
- Soojin Lee (Redwood, Messaging)
- Jordan Blake (Redwood, Sales GTM Sponsor)
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood, NA Field)
- Lukas Meyer (Redwood, EMEA Field)
- Markus Klein (Redwood, SE readiness)
- Jasmine Liu (Redwood, CS)
- Dev Patel (Redwood, Support)
- Claire Dubois (Redwood, Perf/Evals)
- Jonas Weber (Redwood, Methodology Sponsor)
- Elliot Price (Redwood, Docs/Web)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
- Team reviewed launch performance for the Latency/$ Benchmark Report: web traffic, report downloads, signup conversions, and sales pipeline influence.
- Sales shared what talk tracks landed and where prospects pushed back (variance, "my workload is different", region mismatch).
- Support/CS summarized inbound load and top ticket themes; requests for an "official" explanation for why numbers differ.
- Agreed on follow-up experiments: landing page CTA test, methodology deep-dive content, table versioning/changelog, and a refresh cadence proposal.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Funnel metrics and attribution
2) Pipeline + field feedback (NA/EMEA)
3) Support load and escalation themes
4) Methodology / credibility notes
5) Follow-up experiments and owners

Action items (auto-generated)
- Ethan: methodology follow-up + FAQ update
- Tyler: CTA A/B test plan
- Dev: support macros + escalation rubric
- Jordan: collect talk track feedback from field
- Claire: refresh playbook proposal
- Elliot: add versioning / last updated stamp

---

[00:00] Ben Carter: Alright, we’re at time. Thanks everyone. This is the post-launch retro for the benchmark report. Goal today is like, what happened, what worked, what broke, what we do next. Tyler has the metrics, Jordan has pipeline notes, Dev and Jasmine on support load, and Claire/Jonas any methodology follow-ups.

[00:18] Camila Reyes: And just, reminder, this is internal. Let’s be candid. If we accidentally over-claimed anywhere, we fix it. We don’t do the “benchmark war” thing.

[00:26] Talia Benson: I’m taking notes. I’ll send out recap + action items.

[00:31] Ben Carter: Cool. Tyler, you want to start?

[00:34] Tyler Benson: Yep. So, I’m gonna share top-line first, then funnel. Um, launch day through end of week + trailing seven days. For landing page: 182k sessions total, 146k unique users. Peak day was launch day, 71k sessions.

[00:55] Tyler Benson: PDF downloads: 12,480 total. That’s like 6.8% of landing page sessions, which is above our usual gated content benchmark.

[01:06] Ben Carter: Wait, is that unique downloads or events? Because we had that weird double-fire thing.

[01:10] Tyler Benson: Good catch. That’s de-duped on user + 30 min window. Raw events were higher, around 15k.

[01:19] Tyler Benson: Signups: 1,642 new Hosted API signups attributed with UTM to the campaign. That’s strict last-touch. If I do multi-touch in HubSpot, it’s 2,190 influenced signups. Conversion from landing page to signup: 0.9% strict. I think that’s okay given the audience skew (a lot of “read-only” folks, analysts, etc.).

[01:44] Camila Reyes: How does that compare to, like, the previous product launch post?

[01:48] Tyler Benson: That was 0.6% last-touch. So better.

[01:52] Tyler Benson: Meetings booked: 214 total meetings booked via “Talk to us” and “Book a consult” forms that had benchmark UTM in the chain. 83 of those are enterprise / Dedicated or Private interest based on form enrichment and SDR notes.

[02:10] Jordan Blake: I’ll talk about quality in a sec, but the volume’s real.

[02:13] Tyler Benson: Pipeline influenced: this is always squishy. In HubSpot, benchmark campaign influenced $6.4M in open pipeline (opps created within 14 days with any touch). Sourced is $1.1M (first touch). Again, standard caveats.

[02:30] Ben Carter: Tyler can you call out channel mix? What actually drove it.

[02:34] Tyler Benson: Yeah. Social + community was the biggest traffic driver. LinkedIn accounted for 38% of sessions. X was 12%. Organic search already 18% which is kind of wild for week 1, mostly from “latency per dollar” and “LLM inference cost” terms.

[02:53] Tyler Benson: Press/analyst: referrals were 9%, but those had the highest time-on-page and download rate, like 11%.

[03:02] Soojin Lee: SEO note: we should keep the wording stable, avoid changing page title too much.

[03:07] Elliot Price: Agree, but we can update the FAQ and versioning without messing the H1.

[03:12] Ben Carter: Any issues on tracking?

[03:14] Tyler Benson: Minimal. There was a short window where the download link was cached incorrectly for some people in EU—like it returned the older draft PDF. Elliot fixed the cache purge. That was about 27 minutes. I excluded that from “successful download” counting.

[03:33] Elliot Price: Yeah, sorry. CDN got sticky. We’ve got a better invalidation path now.

[03:38] Ben Carter: Okay. Let’s pivot to pipeline and field feedback. Jordan.

[03:43] Jordan Blake: Sure. So, first, it did what we wanted: it gives the team something credible to lead with besides “trust us we’re fast.” AEs used it as an opener and also as a late-stage “here’s methodology.”

[03:58] Jordan Blake: Quality wise, of the 214 meetings Tyler mentioned, we triaged 162 so far. About 40 were students / random newsletter folks. Another ~30 were vendors trying to sell us stuff (lol). But there’s like 60–70 real opportunities, mostly two buckets: AI-native SaaS who are cost sensitive, and enterprise platform teams asking for Dedicated or VPC.

[04:20] Stephanie Nguyen: In NA, the strongest hook was “latency per dollar,” not “lowest cost.” Engineers got it immediately. Procurement folks needed more hand-holding.

[04:30] Lukas Meyer: EMEA, the big thing was data residency. People were like, “Cool chart, but where is it run, what region, and can I keep EU-only.” If we don’t say it clearly, they assume we can’t.

[04:45] Markus Klein: On the SE side, we got a lot of technical questions about caching and batching—like “you optimized for your own harness.” So having the runbook-y explanation helps. But I need a tighter 2-minute explanation for calls.

[05:00] Jordan Blake: Objections that came up repeatedly:
1) “My workload is different, these numbers won’t match.”
2) “Variance: are you cherry-picking runs?”
3) “Cost assumptions: what price did you use, is it list price, is it committed use, etc.”
4) “Region mismatch: I’m in Tokyo / Singapore / Frankfurt, why is my latency not what you show.”

[05:25] Claire Dubois: On (2), we have the variance bands and rerun policy, but it’s buried. People don’t read the appendix.

[05:33] Ethan Wallace: That’s on me. The PDF has it but the landing page summary is too marketing-y. Not intentionally, just… it’s not as explicit.

[05:42] Camila Reyes: We can fix that. We should. Our whole angle is credibility.

[05:47] Ben Carter: Jordan, any competitor mentions? What are we up against in these conversations.

[05:52] Jordan Blake: Together gets mentioned a lot as “we’re evaluating them too.” Replicate sometimes. Hyperscalers: Bedrock for procurement comfort, Azure OpenAI for “we already have contract,” even if they don’t love it. And then the self-host crowd: vLLM, “we’ll just do it ourselves on EKS.”

[06:17] Markus Klein: For self-host, the report helped because we can say: “Yes, you can, but here’s the operational economics and the repeatability.” Still need to be careful not to bash OSS.

[06:30] Ben Carter: Nice. Dev, Jasmine—support and CS load.

[06:35] Dev Patel: Yeah. So launch week we staffed extra. We saw 148 inbound tickets tagged “benchmark/report” over 10 days. That’s higher than normal but manageable. Response times stayed within SLA, except one weekend day where we had a small backlog.

[06:56] Jasmine Liu: CS side, we had a lot of “existing customer saw report and now wants to renegotiate pricing” type questions. Not always bad, but it’s a thing.

[07:05] Dev Patel: Top inbound categories, roughly:
- “How do I reproduce?” (38 tickets)
- “My latency is worse than the chart” (31)
- “What exactly is latency/$ and what cost inputs” (24)
- “Do you store prompts? any customer data used?” (22)
- “What about dedicated/VPC, can you match these SLOs?” (the rest, smaller)

[07:29] Dev Patel: The hardest ones were the mismatch cases. People compare their app end-to-end latency, including network and their own client, to our server-side p50. Then they think we lied.

[07:41] Claire Dubois: That’s the classic. We should label it “server-side model latency” more aggressively.

[07:45] Elliot Price: Landing page currently says “end-to-end latency” in one spot. That might be wrong. I can fix.

[07:51] Ben Carter: Wait, it does? That’s… not ideal.

[07:54] Elliot Price: Yeah, it’s like one sentence in the FAQ. I’ll change it to “API latency measured at Redwood edge” or whatever the approved language is.

[08:03] Jonas Weber: It’s actually measured at the gateway timestamp, not “model only.” But it’s not the customer’s client-to-edge. So we need to phrase carefully.

[08:12] Dev Patel: Also, we need an official macro. Right now agents are stitching together answers from the FAQ and the runbook link. It’s inconsistent.

[08:21] Jasmine Liu: +1. Customers ask in Slack connect too. We need a single canonical answer.

[08:27] Ben Carter: What’s the weirdest ticket.

[08:30] Dev Patel: One prospect asked if the “latency per dollar” metric means we’re like… trading latency for money dynamically. Like, “can I pay more to go faster.” Which, I mean, kinda with Dedicated tiers, but not how the metric is defined.

[08:46] Camila Reyes: That’s actually a messaging issue. We should add a line: it’s a benchmark metric, not a product feature toggle.

[08:52] Soojin Lee: I can update the “explain it to procurement” paragraph.

[08:57] Ben Carter: Claire/Jonas, anything from methodology side we learned? Any real issues or just comms.

[09:03] Claire Dubois: Mostly comms, but two real things:
1) People are very sensitive to caching policy. We said “no prompt caching” and “warmup controlled,” but some readers assumed we were using aggressive prefix caching to juice numbers. Maybe add an explicit bullet: “Caching is disabled except for model weights in GPU memory; no cross-request KV reuse” — or whatever the truth is per workload.

[09:27] Jonas Weber: For chat workload we did allow the standard runtime behaviors that would exist in production, but we did not do cross-user cache reuse. This is where words get tricky.

[09:37] Claire Dubois: Second: APAC region. We included it, but the table is lower on the page and people missed it. We got like 10 questions “do you have Singapore” that are answered on the page.

[09:50] Elliot Price: That’s layout. We can add a “Regions covered” module up top.

[09:55] Ben Carter: Noted.

[09:57] Markus Klein: One more thing: A few technical prospects asked for raw per-request logs. We obviously can’t. But we can offer the reproduction repo. That seems to satisfy them if we are confident it’s easy.

[10:11] Ethan Wallace: The reproduction example is still a little too dev-y. It’s fine for engineers but not for a platform manager. Maybe we need a “five steps to reproduce” doc.

[10:21] Jonas Weber: We should not promise they’ll match exactly. We should say “within a range.” Otherwise we create a support nightmare.

[10:29] Dev Patel: Yes please.

[10:31] Ben Carter: Let’s capture that.

[10:33] Talia Benson: Captured: “how to reproduce” doc, with expectation-setting.

[10:38] Ben Carter: Let’s go back to the funnel. Tyler, where did we lose people? Any drop-off insights.

[10:44] Tyler Benson: Scroll depth: a lot of users got to charts, engaged, but never hit the CTA. There’s a mismatch between “I want the PDF” and “I want to talk to sales.” We put both CTAs but the top fold CTA is “Download PDF.” That’s driving downloads but not necessarily meetings.

[11:06] Ben Carter: So do we want more meetings or more credibility. Like, both, but.

[11:10] Camila Reyes: We need both. But we should not bait-and-switch. If they want a PDF, give them PDF. The sales motion should be optional and obvious.

[11:20] Tyler Benson: Totally. Suggestion is A/B test hero CTA: Variant A stays “Download report.” Variant B is “See results for your region” or “Get a cost/latency consult.” But still provide download below.

[11:34] Soojin Lee: “See results for your region” might reduce the procurement confusion too.

[11:40] Lukas Meyer: Also EMEA forms: we should ask region preference earlier. SDRs are wasting cycles on people who need on-prem or EU-only and we route them incorrectly.

[11:52] Jordan Blake: Yes. Qualification question in the form: “Deployment mode (Hosted, Dedicated, VPC)” and “Primary region.”

[12:00] Ben Carter: Okay. Dev, any other support friction points.

[12:05] Dev Patel: Two. One, security FAQ: we answered “no customer data” but some readers interpret benchmarks as “you used production traffic.” We should say “synthetic prompt sets.” Second, the variance language. People see p95 and then see their p95 is different. They don’t understand concurrency distribution and token lengths.

[12:30] Claire Dubois: We might need a very simple diagram. Like, “we tested short/medium/long prompts, here’s distribution.” The current appendix has numbers but not visually.

[12:40] Ethan Wallace: I can add a small figure. Also maybe add a “common reasons your numbers differ” section.

[12:47] Markus Klein: That would be gold for SEs. Because we’re doing it live on calls now.

[12:53] Ben Carter: Jordan, what talk track worked best.

[12:57] Jordan Blake: The one that lands is: “We’re optimizing for production economics, not leaderboard scores.” Then we show latency/$ plus reliability caveats. When we lead with “we’re cheaper,” people poke holes. When we lead with “predictable and measurable,” it goes smoother.

[13:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Another good one: “Same API across hosted/dedicated/private.” A few enterprise folks used the benchmark as permission to start with hosted while security reviews dedicated.

[13:31] Jasmine Liu: That’s actually important: CS can help with a phased plan. Maybe we should create a template: “start hosted for eval, move to dedicated for SLO, then private for data controls.”

[13:46] Camila Reyes: That’s also content. Could be a follow-up blog or solution brief.

[13:50] Ben Carter: We might be over-scoping. Let’s list follow-ups and prioritize.

[13:56] Talia Benson: I’ll start a stack-ranked list. Keep going.

[14:00] Ben Carter: Ethan, what did we learn about messaging or copy.

[14:03] Ethan Wallace: Two things. The “headline stat” we used—like “X% better latency/$ in region Y”—got the most attention but also the most scrutiny. People asked “better than what.” Even with the disclaimers, it invites comparison fights.

[14:23] Camila Reyes: I’m not surprised.

[14:24] Ethan Wallace: If we do it again, I’d lead with “Here’s the dataset, here’s how to read it, here’s what to do with it.” Less “we win.”

[14:34] Soojin Lee: Agree. The narrative should be “new standard for measuring,” not “we’re number one.”

[14:41] Jordan Blake: Field likes the “we win” slide though.

[14:44] Camila Reyes: Yeah but we can arm field without putting it as the public hero claim. There’s a difference.

[14:52] Markus Klein: We can keep a “competitive appendix” internally. Not on the public page.

[14:58] Ben Carter: Great. Claire, any data quality issues post-launch?

[15:02] Claire Dubois: None that require correction. We had one internal question about a EU-west run that looked off, but it’s within variance. The biggest risk is interpretation, not correctness.

[15:16] Jonas Weber: We should add a table version, like “Benchmark suite v1.2”. So if we rerun later, we can be explicit.

[15:23] Elliot Price: Easy to do. We can stamp “Data collected Feb 2025” and “Methodology v1”.

[15:30] Ben Carter: Alright. Let’s talk experiments. Tyler, list what you want to test.

[15:36] Tyler Benson: Experiments:
- CTA hero A/B as mentioned.
- Form friction: add 2 fields vs. none; see if conversion drops but meeting quality improves.
- Retargeting: run a small paid retargeting to people who downloaded but didn’t sign up.
- Email nurture: we sent 3 touches. Open rates were good (42%, 38%, 35%), but click-through dropped on email 3. We might need a technical deep dive email earlier.

[16:05] Ben Carter: Ben the growth person wants more tests, shocking.

[16:08] Tyler Benson: Guilty.

[16:10] Camila Reyes: I’m okay with tests as long as we keep the credibility bar. No dark patterns.

[16:16] Ben Carter: Sales follow-ups? Jordan.

[16:19] Jordan Blake: We should do a short SE-led webinar: “How to interpret latency/$ for your stack.” Not a product pitch. That’s a good middle-of-funnel.

[16:31] Markus Klein: I’ll do it if we have a tight deck and we don’t get into competitor bashing.

[16:37] Lukas Meyer: Time zone friendly for EMEA too. Maybe two sessions.

[16:43] Jasmine Liu: And we should have a “what happens after you book a consult” guide. People book and then ghost. If we set expectations, show them we’ll run a mini-benchmark of their prompt distribution, they show up.

[16:58] Ben Carter: Support follow-ups, Dev.

[17:01] Dev Patel: Two macros: “numbers differ” and “reproduce.” Also, we need a standard escalation path because Owen got pulled into like five threads ad hoc.

[17:12] Owen Phillips: (joins late) Sorry, was on another call. Yeah I got pinged a bunch. If we define “only escalate if X,” it’ll help.

[17:20] Dev Patel: Exactly.

[17:23] Ben Carter: Great timing, Owen. What do you need.

[17:26] Owen Phillips: A checklist: what to ask the customer for (region, model, token lengths, concurrency, streaming on/off, sdk version) before it hits tier 3.

[17:38] Claire Dubois: We can align that with the reproduction doc so it’s consistent.

[17:44] Ben Carter: Okay.

[17:46] Talia Benson: Captured: create “info required for escalation” template.

[17:52] Ben Carter: Now, the elephant: refresh cadence. We teased “we’ll update.” What do we mean.

[17:59] Camila Reyes: We can’t do this every month. It was a lot.

[18:03] Claire Dubois: Yeah, the benchmark windows alone were heavy. We can do quarterly or “major model family release” triggered.

[18:12] Jonas Weber: I’d propose: quarterly scheduled refresh for stability, plus ad hoc update if a major region or runtime change materially shifts results.

[18:25] Tyler Benson: From marketing standpoint, quarterly is good. We can do “Q2 2025 edition.” Creates an ongoing story.

[18:33] Jordan Blake: Sales loves fresh numbers, but also hates moving targets. If we refresh, we need a change log so old decks don’t become “wrong.”

[18:44] Elliot Price: Versioning solves this. We can keep old versions accessible with a note.

[18:50] Markus Klein: Please keep old versions. Otherwise prospects say, “why did you delete it.”

[18:55] Ben Carter: Great. Any other lessons learned.

[18:59] Soojin Lee: One. The phrase “latency per dollar” is not standard. Engineers like it, finance folks ask “dollars of what.” Next time we might also phrase as “tokens/sec per $” or “p50 latency at $/1M tokens.” But that’s jargon. Maybe we need a glossary.

[19:20] Camila Reyes: A glossary section in the PDF could help without cluttering.

[19:25] Ethan Wallace: I can add it. Lightweight.

[19:28] Ben Carter: Okay. Let’s do a quick round: NA/EMEA/Support/Docs—what’s one thing you want fixed this week.

[19:36] Stephanie Nguyen: One-pager for procurement. They ask “what does this mean for contract.” Right now AEs improvise.

[19:44] Lukas Meyer: Region + residency language. Put it on top. And don’t say “global” without qualifiers.

[19:52] Dev Patel: Official support macro for mismatch and a single canonical link to send.

[19:58] Elliot Price: Version stamp + fix that “end-to-end” wording. Also move regions coverage higher.

[20:06] Markus Klein: Two-minute talk track. Like literally a script: what’s measured, what’s not, how to reproduce.

[20:15] Claire Dubois: I want the “common reasons differ” section so I stop answering the same question.

[20:21] Jonas Weber: Ensure we don’t accidentally claim we used production traffic. “Synthetic prompt sets” should be explicit.

[20:30] Ben Carter: Great. Now let’s talk about the nurture emails quickly. Tyler said CTR dropped. What did we send.

[20:38] Tyler Benson: Email 1 was announcement. Email 2 was “methodology overview.” Email 3 was “model spotlight.” The feedback from a few recipients was they wanted “how do I apply this to my app” sooner.

[20:54] Jordan Blake: Yes, because the skeptical people don’t care about our charts, they care about “will it work for me.”

[21:01] Jasmine Liu: CS can help craft a checklist: “Bring these 3 inputs and we’ll estimate your cost/latency.” That can be the CTA.

[21:13] Ben Carter: That sounds like the webinar / consult flow.

[21:17] Camila Reyes: But be careful we don’t imply we’ll do free consulting for everybody. We need criteria.

[21:24] Jordan Blake: SDRs can qualify. We can say “for teams above X volume.”

[21:30] Ben Carter: Okay.

[21:32] Talia Benson: I’ll note: define qualification for “mini-benchmark consult.”

[21:37] Ben Carter: Any negative press or backlash.

[21:40] Camila Reyes: Not backlash, but some snark on X about “marketing benchmarks.” We responded politely with methodology link. It actually drove more traffic.

[21:51] Ethan Wallace: One thread accused us of hiding confidence intervals. We do show them, but they’re small. We might want to show them more visibly.

[22:02] Claire Dubois: Showing the band more prominently might look like we’re less confident though.

[22:07] Jonas Weber: It’s a trade. But credibility is the goal. I’d rather show it.

[22:12] Ben Carter: We can add an “uncertainty / variance” callout box. Doesn’t need to be huge.

[22:18] Elliot Price: On web, we can add a “How stable are these results?” accordion.

[22:22] Ben Carter: Great.

[22:24] Owen Phillips: Sorry quick—on mismatch tickets, sometimes it’s routing. People hit a different region than they think. Can we add docs about the region header again.

[22:33] Elliot Price: There’s already a region header doc but it’s buried in OpenAI compat. I can cross-link from benchmark page.

[22:40] Markus Klein: Please. This comes up constantly.

[22:43] Ben Carter: Okay, we’re getting near time. Let’s recap decisions.

[22:48] Ben Carter: Decision 1: We will do versioning + last-updated stamps on page and tables.

[22:54] Ben Carter: Decision 2: We will create a “common reasons your numbers differ” section and support macros.

[23:00] Ben Carter: Decision 3: We’ll run CTA A/B test and potentially add qualification fields.

[23:05] Ben Carter: Decision 4: We propose quarterly refresh cadence with changelog, pending exec sign-off.

[23:11] Camila Reyes: And decision 5: keep claims conservative publicly; competitive framing stays mostly internal.

[23:18] Ben Carter: Yes.

[23:20] Talia Benson: Action items I captured, I’ll send out. Anything I missed.

[23:25] Jordan Blake: Add: collect field feedback examples. I’ll do that.

[23:29] Ethan Wallace: I’ll draft the methodology follow-up post. Need Jonas and Claire to review.

[23:35] Jonas Weber: Yep.

[23:36] Claire Dubois: Yep.

[23:37] Dev Patel: And I’ll update macros + ask Owen for the escalation checklist fields.

[23:43] Owen Phillips: I’ll send you a list today.

[23:46] Ben Carter: Great. Any last thoughts.

[23:49] Lukas Meyer: Just: for EMEA, avoid US-centric language in examples. Like “us-east.” Put EU examples too.

[23:56] Soojin Lee: Good point.

[23:58] Camila Reyes: Thanks all. This was a big cross-functional push. Let’s keep the momentum but also let people breathe.

[24:05] Ben Carter: Alright, done. Talia will send recap. Thanks.

[24:09] Meeting ended.

---
Note: Transcript generated by Fireflies.ai. Some words may be mis-transcribed (e.g., region names, product names, acronyms).
